query: Reported superconducting high-entropy alloys are dominated by Nb-Ta matrices, while other studies concern titanium-rich systems based on heavy transition metals and partly ordered systems. Consequently, these precedents do not establish what controls superconductivity in high-entropy alloys outside the best-studied material classes. Within the defining constraint of a solid solution containing at least five elements at no less than 5 atomic percent each, what governs superconducting behavior in such an uncharacterized high-entropy alloy, and why? State one testable mechanistic hypothesis, a controlled comparison against the starting material, predicted observations relative to the baseline, applicable boundary conditions, the earlier evidence supporting the hypothesis, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In a fully disordered, equiatomic high‐entropy superconductor (with at least five elements all above 5 at.%), the superconducting transition temperature is primarily governed by the average valence electron concentration (VEC), which tunes the density of states and thus the electron–phonon coupling. At the same time, the inherent lattice distortions (from chemical disorder) modulate scattering rates. A controlled alteration in VEC without introducing secondary phases can therefore systematically modify Tc.
generation.material_initial_state: A single‐phase solid solution high‐entropy alloy that is not based on the well‐studied Nb–Ta matrix—for example, a Ti-rich, heavy transition metal HEA with equiatomic or near‐equiatomic composition (each element ≥5 at.%) and a BCC or FCC structure as confirmed by XRD.
generation.intervention: Substitute a small fraction (e.g., ~5 at.%) of one constituent with an element of nearly the same atomic size but different valence electron count. This maintains the disordered single-phase state while incrementally increasing or decreasing the overall VEC.
generation.conditions: Samples are synthesized under identical conditions (e.g., via arc melting or high-energy mechanical milling followed by sintering) to ensure similar microstructure and phase purity. Superconducting properties (Tc) are measured via four-probe resistivity in a cryogenic environment (1.5–20 K) under vacuum or inert atmosphere.
generation.structural_mediator: The electronic density of states at the Fermi level, as modulated by the average valence electron count and the degree of lattice distortion produced by chemical disorder, which governs the electron–phonon coupling strength.
generation.mechanism: A higher (or lower) VEC alters the density of states available for pairing, thereby changing the electron–phonon coupling that drives superconductivity. Chemical disorder, while intrinsic to the HEA, affects local lattice strains and electron scattering. The balance between these factors sets the observed Tc.
generation.predicted_outcome: An alloy modified to have a higher VEC (through the controlled substitution) is predicted to exhibit a higher superconducting transition temperature relative to the baseline. Conversely, a substitution that lowers VEC should reduce Tc, establishing a systematic correlation.
generation.baseline: The as-synthesized, equiatomic high-entropy alloy with a known Tc measured under identical conditions.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies as long as the alloy remains a single-phase, disordered solid solution (i.e., no secondary precipitates or significant phase segregation) and within a VEC range typical for metallic superconductors (roughly 4–7 electrons).
generation.uncertainty: The precise magnitude of the Tc change is uncertain due to the complex interplay between enhanced electron–phonon coupling from increased VEC and potential increases in scattering from lattice distortions. Quantitative calibration will be needed.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of samples: (a) a baseline equiatomic high-entropy alloy (unmodified) and (b) a series in which one element is partially substituted (≈5 at.%) by an element of similar atomic size but differing VEC, with all samples prepared identically. Confirm single-phase structure via XRD and microstructural homogeneity via electron microscopy. Measure the superconducting transition temperature (Tc) with four-probe resistivity measurements in a controlled cryostat (1.5–20 K).
measurements: Electron microscopy (assess chemical disorder and microstructure)
Energy dispersive spectroscopy (verify composition and VEC)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If changing the VEC by controlled substitution does not lead to a measurable and systematic change in Tc beyond experimental uncertainties—or if secondary phases form that independently affect Tc—then the hypothesis that VEC (modulated by disorder-induced lattice distortions) governs superconducting behavior in these HEAs would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In 2014, the first superconducting high-entropy alloy Ta0.34Nb0.33Hf0.08Zr0.14Ti0.11 (in at.%) was discovered []. According to Sun and Cava [], this alloy can be classified as a type-A HEA superconductor. HEAs of this type contain only metals on the left side of the transition metal region of the periodic table, crystallize in a body-centered cubic (bcc) lattice, and exhibit superconducting transition temperatures (Tc) between 4.0 and 9.2 K, while their highest upper critical field (μ0Hc2) is close to 12 T [,,,,,,]. These are the most widely studied HEA superconductors to date. However, it should be noted that most of these alloys contain a large amount of niobium and tantalum, while the titanium concentration is typically less than 20 at.%. Because binary Nb-Ti alloys exhibit much better superconducting properties than Nb-Ta [], it is plausible to expect that NbTi-based high-entropy alloys will have a higher Tc and/or μ0Hc2 compared to previously reported type-A HEA superconductors. Moreover, in the case of various ternary Nb-Ti-Hf and Nb-Ti-Ta and quaternary Nb-Ti-Ta-Hf alloys, the highest values of μ0Hc2 were observed for the titanium-rich alloys []. It has long been recognized that a critical amount of disorder can suppress superconductivity near the Anderson quantum phase transition. The observed Tc reduction concomitant with a mixing entropy ΔS enhancement in superconducting HEAs seems to agree with that picture. On the other hand, recent analyses of competing interaction-channels in strongly disordered metals predict a Tc enhancement within the BCS framework, when the electron system is tuned to a quantum critical point,. This hypothesis finds support in a recent study of HEA (TaNb)1-x(HfZrTi)x thin films; while each of the binary alloys TaNb and HfZrTi does not show a superconducting transition at or above 2 K, all solid solutions of (TaNb)1-x(HfZrTi)x at various mixing ratios x are superconducting at Tc≤6.9 K. This ’cocktail’ effect suggests an intricate relation between the presence of strong compositional disorder, realized through the random arrangement of five atomic species on a bcc lattice, and superconductivity, which is an interesting question to address experimentally.
